mcqs.question: Two engineers benchmark the same function on the same machine and get results that differ by 40%. Neither changed the code. What is the most likely cause?
options: The benchmark tool itself is broken and needs replacing
One of them included cold-start/JIT-warm-up iterations or ran on a noisy machine, while the other controlled for it
Benchmarks are inherently random and this variance is expected and unavoidable
The function has a race condition that produces different timings on different runs
mcqs.explanation: Uncontrolled warm-up and environment noise (shared machine load, cold caches) routinely produce 10-40% swings between otherwise-identical runs. This isn't randomness to shrug off or a tooling bug — it's exactly what controlling for warm-up and noise is meant to eliminate.

mcqs.question: A microbenchmark shows algorithm A is 2x faster than algorithm B in isolation. What can you conclude about their behavior inside the full production system?
options: A will still be roughly 2x faster once deployed, since Big-O and microbenchmarks predict system behavior
Nothing about their relative performance is safely knowable until this is validated with a system-level benchmark
B is actually faster in production, since microbenchmarks typically invert the real ranking
The 2x figure only applies to single-threaded environments and is meaningless otherwise
mcqs.explanation: A microbenchmark isolates one operation and can't see contention, cache effects, or interactions with the rest of the system that a system-level benchmark would surface. The isolated win might survive, shrink, or reverse — a microbenchmark alone can't tell you which without a system-level check.

mcqs.question: Why do JIT-compiled languages (Java, JavaScript via V8, .NET) need a dedicated warm-up phase before a benchmark's measurement begins?
options: Warm-up allocates memory the benchmark will need later
It gives the operating system time to schedule the process on a faster CPU core
The runtime initially runs unoptimized code and only recompiles hot functions to optimized native code after enough invocations, so early iterations measure the wrong performance regime
It's a superstition carried over from older hardware and isn't actually necessary on modern machines
mcqs.explanation: JIT runtimes profile execution and recompile hot paths into optimized code only after observing enough calls, so measuring from the first invocation captures interpreter/baseline performance that can be 5-10x slower than steady state. Discarding warm-up iterations is what makes the measured number represent real long-running performance.

mcqs.question: Two versions of a function both report a mean latency of 14ms across a benchmark run. Why might reporting only the mean be misleading?
options: Means are always mathematically incorrect for timing data
One version could have a long tail (occasional very slow runs) that the mean hides, while the other has a tight, consistent distribution — very different real experiences with the same mean
The mean should never be computed for fewer than a million samples
Latency data cannot be averaged because it isn't normally distributed
mcqs.explanation: Two distributions can share an identical mean while one has a long tail of slow outliers and the other doesn't — exactly the average-vs-tail trap. Reporting percentiles (p50, p95, p99) alongside the mean, and ideally a variance figure, is what exposes that difference.

mcqs.question: A micro-benchmark of a string-processing loop reports an unexpectedly tiny elapsed time — far faster than the operation should plausibly take. What's the most likely explanation?
options: String operations really can be that fast on modern hardware
The compiler or JIT proved the loop's result was never used and eliminated it as dead code, so the benchmark measured almost nothing
The system clock used for timing has insufficient resolution to measure such fast operations
The benchmark ran on more CPU cores than expected, parallelizing the loop automatically
mcqs.explanation: If a loop's output is never read, an optimizing compiler is free to remove it entirely — the benchmark then times an empty loop and reports a suspiciously fast result. The fix is forcing the result to be observed (returned, printed, or via a tool like JMH's Blackhole), not assuming the code is genuinely that fast.

mcqs.question: A service's p99 latency has crept up 20% over three months, but no single commit's benchmark ever showed an alarming regression. What benchmarking practice is designed to catch exactly this?
options: Running a single large system-level benchmark right before each major release
Increasing the number of repetitions in one-off microbenchmarks
Adding more percentiles to the one-off benchmark's report
Regression benchmarking — tracking the metric on every commit so small, individually-invisible creeps accumulate visibly over time
mcqs.explanation: A one-off benchmark, however careful, only ever compares two points in time — it can't catch a slow creep spread across many small commits, none of which individually crosses an alert threshold. Continuous regression benchmarking tracks the trend, which is the only way to see the accumulated 20% before it becomes an incident.
